Notes from my Gardening/ Hobby Farm Journal-
February 2
Today I created my first "seed snail" after watching dozens of TikTok videos over how this was a superior way to start plants from seeds. It takes minimal effort, space, and can be done indoors. Over the past year, I have started a small hobby farm including chickens and rabbits, so I have many empty feed bags I have been collecting in preparation to start the seed snails. I cut the feed bags into strips about 4 inches tall and the full length of the bag. The only other supplies you need are potting soil, seeds(I picked non GMO and Heirloom so I could hopefully save my own seeds to plant next year), and something to secure the bag with. I used packing tape because that is what I had on hand. However, the packing tape did not stick that well due to how damp everything was. Duct tape, rubber bands, or twine would have been easier to work with. I started with 8 seed packets. I picked the seeds of four plants I use a lot when cooking and let my kids pick the other four. I have roma tomato, cucumber, squash, watermelon, cantaloupe, carrot, lettuce, and bell pepper. To assemble the seed snails- roll out a strip of the feed bag, pack potting soil from edge to edge about 1/2 inch deep. Roll the strip tightly and secure the end so it does not uncurl. I placed the seed snails on a plastic tray and placed in front of a window in a spare room that faces the sun all day long. I watered the seed snails from the top and stopped watering when the water soaked through to the bottom of the seed snail.
February 11th
Waiting to see signs of growth was very exciting and also caused a little anxiety. I bought all of the seeds from Amazon as a large seed mix. Overall, the reviews were good, but I was still worried I had gotten a bad batch or the conditions wouldn't be right for spouting. The carrot plant and the lettuce plant were the plant that sprouted first. Those are now the tallest plants. I noticed the soil seemed to be drying out too fast and I was worried about watering to frequently because I had read root rot could be more prevalent in plants grown using this technique.. After watching a few TikTok videos, I decided to cover the top of each seed snail with a gallon zip lock bag. The videos I watched said that the bags would help keep the plants moist by trapping in the moisture that would otherwise evaporate. The zip lock bags were also supposed to help keep the soil warmer. Some videos mentioned placing the plants on a heating pad but my electricity bill is already so high that I do not want to do that unless I absolutely have to. I changed the way I was watering; I started watering the tray and not the plants. I fill the tray up with about a half inch of water and let the water soak the soil from the base of the seed snail to the top. I think that has made the biggest difference, because in the last few days I have noticed a lot more baby sprouts. 
February 19th
I had a small mishap yesterday. It was very disappointing, because this plant was growing so well and it was the only variation of this plant I had planted. There were several warm days in Oklahoma, so I moved the tray of seed snails from inside to outside on the porch so they could get more direct light in the evenings too. Last night when, I went to move the tray of seed snails back indoors the watermelon seed snail flipped off the tray and landed top down on the ground. Several of the plants snapped in half, and two dislodged from the soil all together. I placed those back in the soil. There were not a lot of roots in tact but I am hoping they will grow so more roots and thrive. I checked on the plants this morning and they look rough. Some are wilted and brown already and some are a lighter green. I am going to be realistic and say that most likely only two of the watermelon plants will make it, if any of them do. 
February 28th
Very busy day, but here is an update on the watermelon plants: Only one plant made it. I am crushed, but it is just Feb. 28th. I will have to start over with water melon seeds, but there IS time. On the bright side, everything else has sprouted and looks healthy. I realized when planting that seeds come in so many shapes and sizes, even colors! However, I never really thought about the plants as they sprout. The plants are all green of course, butt he leaves and stalk are all different.
March 2nd
Since this was my first year I was not really sure what I was doing and I was not confident that the seeds would sprout. Some of the seed snails are overfull due to this. I think the carrot seed packet had close to 100 seeds. The way this seed snail looked, I bet all 100 seeds sprouted! Today i had to very carefully unroll the lettuce and the carrots. I had to go slow and untangle plants as I went. Once it was all untangled and flat I then added more potting soil to the "snail" along with some rabbit manure before rolling back up. This adds more room so they won't continue to get more tangled and it adds more room for root growth too.
March 5th
I noticed some of the leaves had become faded in some spots. After researching it a bit I realized the potting soil I chose did not have a lot of added fertilizer. I am trying to be as organic as possible with my garden, so I'm not adding synthetic or store bought fertilizer. I have rabbits and chickens. The manure from both animals can be used to boost the growth of plants. HOWEVER, chicken manure is considered a hot manure and cannot be placed directly onto he plants, it will come them. Rabbit manure is the opposite. The cold manure can be added directly to the soil when plating. I soaked rabbit manure in a bucket of water and have been watering the plants with it. It seems to have perked the plants up more and I have seen some new growth.
March 10th
Since things have been going well and the first plants are thriving, today after work I created seed snails for the rest of the seeds I had on hand. I was able to fill two more trays with seed snails. Now I have a total of 29 fruit and vegetables started. I have not forgotten about the watermelon seeds. I just have not made it to the store yet. I added more soild toall the seed snails that looed like the plants were overwhelming the space. Space is limited inside when the weather is cold, so I purchased a small greenhouse. This will not only be great for the growth of the plants during the seed snail phase, but will help them grow better when I replant them into individual planters. We have a lot of deer and rabbits in our area. Those animals can eat you garden in a manner of days if they are left unchecked.


March 12
The greenhouse I ordered arrived today in a long narrow box. I was honestly surprised how small the box was considering it was supposed to be a whole greenhouse. I waited until after dinner to open it because I knew my kids would want to “help,” which usually means twice the time and half the progress. When I opened the box, everything was in a lot of small pieces. It came with metal poles, plastic connectors, shelves, and a green plastic cover. I spent a few minutes just laying everything out on the grass so I could make sure nothing was missing. The directions said assembly should take about 30 minutes. I knew right away that probably was not going to be the case. The first step was connecting the bottom frame pieces together using the plastic corner joints. The pieces were labeled with small stickers, which helped a lot. The kids wanted to snap the pieces together, which actually worked out because some of the joints were pretty tight.Once the base was finished, I started building the vertical supports and then the shelves. The shelves are wire racks that sit across the frame pieces. The instructions showed four shelves total.
About halfway through building it, I realized one of the support bars had been put in upside down, which meant I had to partially take it back apart and fix it. That part was frustrating, but once it was corrected everything started fitting together better. After about an hour, we had the frame finished. It actually looked pretty sturdy for something that was mostly thin metal tubing. The last step was sliding the green plastic cover over the frame. This part was harder than expected because the cover was a tight fit. The kids thought it was funny watching me try to wrestle the plastic down over the top corners. Eventually we got it into place and zipped the front door closed. Standing back and looking at it, I felt pretty proud. It may be small, but it feels like a big step toward making the garden more organized. Tomorrow I will start moving some of the seed snails into it.

March 14
Today after work I started moving some of the trays of seed snails into the greenhouse. I didn’t want to move all of them at once until I could see how the temperature and moisture levels behaved inside.The greenhouse is sitting on the back porch where it gets a lot of sunlight during the afternoon. When I unzipped the door after it had been sitting in the sun for a while, I could already tell the inside felt warmer than the outside air. I placed one tray of the strongest plants on the middle shelf and another tray on the lower shelf. The top shelf seemed like it might get too warm at first, so I decided to leave that one empty for now. One thing I noticed pretty quickly was that the greenhouse holds humidity really well. After watering the plants, the inside of the plastic cover started forming small droplets of condensation. That actually made me feel better about moving them outside because it means the plants should stay moist without me having to water them constantly. I checked on them again before dark and everything still looked good.
March 16
The plants that I moved into the greenhouse seem to be doing well so far. If anything, they look a little perkier than the ones still inside the house.One thing I did notice today is that the greenhouse can heat up pretty quickly when the sun is strong. It felt really nice with the door flap zipped closed.I’m thinking I may bring a lawn chair to place inside the greenhouse so I can read out here sometimes.But then when I checked on it around lunchtime, it felt almost too warm inside. Because of that, I decided to unzip the door part way during the day so some of the heat could escape. I don’t want the plants to cook inside there.Gardening definitely seems like a constant balancing act between too much and too little of everything.

March 18
Today I moved the rest of the seed snails into the greenhouse. The shelves are now almost completely full. Seeing all the trays lined up together made me realize just how many plants I actually started. Twenty-nine seed snails  seemed like a good starting number when I first planted the seeds, but now that they are growing it looks like a lot. I’m starting to realize I may have planted more than our garden space can realistically hold.That might mean I end up giving some plants away to friends or neighbors later on.

March 21
The greenhouse has been working really well so far. The plants are definitely growing faster now that they are getting more sunlight. The tomato plants especially seem to be taking off. Several of them have already grown tall enough that they are starting to lean slightly toward the light. I rotated the trays today so that different sides of the plants face the sun. I read that doing this can help keep them from growing crooked.I also checked the soil levels in some of the seed snails and added a little more potting soil where needed.

March 24
Today I finally made it to the store and bought new watermelon seeds to replace the ones that were mostly lost in the accident a few weeks ago. This time I decided to start them in a shorter seed snail just to make sure it is not top heavy. I do not want to destroy another roll of plants again. Next time, I may not have time to get them started.. I’m hoping this will make it easier to manage them and avoid overcrowding, too. It feels a little funny starting new seeds when the other plants are already growing so well, but I really want to have watermelons this summer.

March 26
I checked on the greenhouse this morning before leaving for work and noticed something interesting. The plants that are on the middle shelves seem to be growing slightly faster than the ones on the bottom shelves. My guess is that they are getting the best balance of sunlight and warmth in that spot. Because of that, I moved some of the slow growing plants up to the middle shelf and rotated the fast growing ones down. I am starting to realize that even within a small greenhouse, plant layout can make a difference.

March 30
Today was one of those days where I really felt like the garden is starting to come together. Many of the plants now have several sets of leaves, and some of them are beginning to look like real garden plants instead of tiny sprouts. I spent some time researching when each plant should be transplanted into the outdoor garden beds. It sounds like most of them will need to stay inside the greenhouse for a few more weeks until the risk of frost is completely gone. In the meantime, I plan to start preparing the outdoor garden space. I have a battery operated tiller that will make easy work of it, I think.

April 2
This afternoon I started working on clearing the garden area in the yard. Last year this spot was mostly just grass and weeds, but 20 years ago it was a family garden plot. I used a shovel and rake to loosen the soil and remove some of the bigger weeds. It was harder work than I expected. At one point I looked back toward the porch and saw the greenhouse sitting there with all the little plants growing inside. It reminded me why I started all of this in the first place. Even though gardening has already come with some trial and error, it has also been really rewarding to see things grow. After the bigger rocks and roots had been moved away, I had my husband bring the tiller over answer took turns tilling the land that had went untouched for the better part of 20 years.


April 4
There was a  gnat problem but it to be improving after reducing the watering time. It made me realize how quickly small environmental changes can affect the plants. The tomatoes continue to grow the fastest. Some of them are already tall enough that they will probably need support once they move outside.

April 8
The weather has been getting warmer lately, which means I’ll soon need to start thinking about moving the plants outside. However, I’ve read that plants need to be “hardened off” before being transplanted outdoors. That means gradually exposing them to outdoor conditions so they don’t go into shock. Since I learned my lesson about that earlier when some plants wilted, I want to do it the right way this time. It seems like I am learning something new every day.

April 10
Today I started the hardening off process. I placed several trays of plants outside the greenhouse for about an hour in the late afternoon. The sunlight and breeze are stronger outside, so I didn’t want to leave them out too long the first day. After bringing them back in, the plants still looked healthy. If everything goes well, I’ll increase the amount of outdoor time each day. It literally feels like I am babysitting plants.

April 14
The plants have now spent several days slowly increasing their time outdoors. There hasn’t been a frost in weeks. So far they seem to be handling it well. The stems actually look a little sturdier after experiencing the wind. I’m beginning to feel more confident that they will survive once transplanted and we may be able to have a successful garden thi year. The local community center has just announced they are going to start holding a farmers market. Maybe we will have some vegetables to sell soon.
April 18
Today I started marking out rows in the garden area.I used stakes and string to visualize where the plants will go. Some plants need more space than others, especially the squash and watermelon. Looking at the rows made the garden feel much more real. My rows weren’t exactly parallel, but I think it should be fine.

April 22
When I was checking on the garden area this morning, I noticed something that reminded me why people talk about protecting their gardens from animals. A rabbit darted into the bushes across from the broken fence and there were several deer tracks near the edge of the yard. If the deer find the garden once the plants are in the ground, I bet they could eat most of it in one night. There are two fruit trees near the garden plot, so the deer are going to be drawn to that area no matter what. My only option was to make sure nothing could get in. I spent the afternoon and evening making sure all the fence poles were sturdy and tacking up any loose pieces of the chicken wire fencing. 

April 26
Today was the big day. I finally transplanted the first plants into the garden. I think some of my excitement even rubbed off on the kids. They are getting more excited about helping. Gardening is becoming something we can do together; it is not just something that feels like a chore.  I started with a few of the strongest tomato plants. Digging the holes felt strangely exciting after spending so many weeks caring for them inside. After planting them, I added a little rabbit manure to the soil and watered them deeply. Seeing the plants in the ground made the garden feel like it was finally beginning. I have to admit I'm glad I won’t have to mess with the tomato plant seed snails anymore. The plants were getting tangled and constantly weighing each other down. They have a lot more room in the garden.

April 30
The transplanted tomatoes are still standing strong after several days. I bought some stakes for when they get tall enough that the tomatoes weigh the plant down, but I do not think I will need to worry about that for at least a month. I kind of feel silly about feeling so nervous to move them now. Learning a new skill is always nerve wracking, but this new task felt especially important. The main goal in starting it was learning how to be self reliant so I could pass that down to my children. There are still many more plants waiting in the greenhouse, but now that I know the process works I feel much more confident about the next round of transplanting.

May 4
Over the past few days I have been gradually transplanting more plants from the greenhouse into the garden. The peppers and cucumbers were the first thing I planted after the tomatoes. We eat a lot of those and I wanted to get them growing vegetables as soon as possible. I decided to move them in smaller groups rather than all at once just in case something went wrong. Digging the holes is definitely the most time-consuming part and the hardest on my back if I am being honest. After doing one row, I asked my son to help. He has a shovel for metal detecting that is the perfect height for him. He would dig the small hole after I marked where it needed to be.  tried to space the plants out according to the recommendations I found online, but I also had to work around the space I actually have available in the garden plot. Once he dug the hole I would break the roots a little on the root ball so that they would anchor into the ground better and then palace in the hole. My daughters would then come behind me and one would backfill the plant with dirt and the other would water the plant. The cucumbers looked a little droopy right after transplanting, which made me nervous at first. I watered them well and added a small layer of mulch around the base of each plant to help the soil hold moisture. By the next morning they looked much better. The cucumbers and squash are what grew the best in my raised garden bed last year. That is until the squash beetles found them. I will have to keep a close eye on the pests this year. Especially since I am hoping to be all organic. The bell peppers seem to be adjusting really well so far. Their leaves are still a deep green and the stems feel strong. I am hoping that is a good sign that they handled the transplant process without too much stress. One thing I have started noticing more is how different each type of plant grows. The tomatoes seem to grow taller quickly, while the peppers stay shorter and bushier. The cucumbers look like they are already trying to spread outward instead of upward.Gardening is definitely teaching me patience. Things change slowly, but every day there seems to be something new to notice.

May 9
Today I noticed something exciting while checking the garden in the morning. Several of the tomato plants have started developing small yellow flowers. I knew that tomatoes would eventually flower, but seeing it actually happen felt like a milestone. It means the plants are moving into the next stage of growth. I spent some time reading about how tomato flowers eventually turn into fruit. Apparently they rely on wind or insects to help with pollination. That made me realize I might want to plant some flowers nearby later to help attract pollinators like bees. The cucumbers are also starting to spread more across the soil. I may need to build a small trellis or support for them so they have something to climb. Every time I check the garden now I feel a little more confident that this new hobby/ skill  might actually work.

May 14
The garden has been doing well overall, but today I noticed my first real problem. Some of the leaves on the squash plants have small holes in them. At first I thought maybe it was just damage from wind, but after looking closer I realized something has definitely been chewing on them.I checked underneath a few of the leaves and saw a couple of small green caterpillars. They were not very big, but it was clear they were responsible for the damage. Honestly I was just happy it was not he sq uash bug. Caterpillars amy be just as hard to get rid of, though. I will do some research later on what natural things I can do to get rid of the caterpillars. For now, we picked off all of the caterpillars we could find and through them in the chicken coop. The chickens loved the caterpillars! It did take a little while to check each plant carefully, bit it will be worth it if we can avoid using chemicals in the garden. Before calling it a night, I watered the plants and made a note to keep checking them over the next few days.This is another part of gardening I hadn’t thought much about before. The seed snails were safe from everything indoors, but when you grow plants outside, you are sharing the space with a lot of other living things that might want to eat them.

May 18
The caterpillar problem seems to be under control for now. I have continued checking the plants each evening and removing any new ones that appear. On another positive note, the tomato plants are continuing to grow quickly. I think sometimes they grow and inch or more in just a day. I need to start measuring them and keeping track. Some of them are now tall enough that I added the stakes I bought earlier.I gently tied the main stems to the stakes using some soft garden ties so the plants would stay upright. It felt strange at first to tie the plants like that, but it makes sense considering how heavy they will eventually become once they start producing tomatoes. I didn’t tie them too tight, since the stalk of the plant will need room to thicken and grow up the stake. I guess I will need to undo the ties and retie as the plant grows. Just one more thing I never thought of before now that I will need to research. The cucumbers have also started sending out little curling tendrils. These seem to grab onto anything nearby for support. They are planted close enough to the fencing that I have started some of the plant tendrils climbing up. I may have to go back and support the fence if the plant becomes too heavy for it. Watching how plants naturally try to climb and spread is really interesting. It’s something I never paid attention to before.

May 23
Today I noticed the first tiny cucumbers forming behind some of the flowers. They are extremely small right now, but you can clearly see the shape starting to develop.Seeing actual vegetables forming on the plants made the whole garden feel more real. Up until now it has mostly been leaves and stems growing bigger.I also checked the watermelon plants that I restarted in the greenhouse earlier. They are finally strong enough that I think they will be ready to transplant soon. Hopefully this second attempt goes a little smoother than the first one.

May 27
The watermelon plants were transplanted into the garden today. I chose a spot along the edge where they will have plenty of space to spread out. This area sits a little lower than the rest of the garden too so any runoff water from water the plants or from the rain will settle here and keep the plants extra moist. Since watermelon vines can grow quite large, I made sure to leave extra room between them and the other plants. Of all the things we planted, my son is most excited about the watermelon. I will take extra care of these plants for sure. The soil in that part of the garden felt nice and loose, which should help their roots spread easily. I added a little rabbit manure to each planting hole and watered them deeply. Transplanting these plants made me think back to the accident earlier in the season when the first watermelon seed snail fell off the tray. At the time it felt like a big setback, but restarting them wasn’t nearly as difficult as I expected. That experience has probably been one of the biggest lessons so far. Even when something goes wrong in the garden, there is often still time to try again. Packs of seeds are so inexpensive compared to buying the actual plants from a nursery. There is a lot more room for trial and error when the start-up cost is not as steep.

June 1
Today I picked the first vegetables from the garden. Two cucumbers had grown large enough to harvest, so I clipped them from the vine. They were not very big, but they looked fresh and healthy. Bringing them inside felt surprisingly rewarding. After months of planting, watering, adjusting, and learning, it was exciting to finally see a result that we could actually eat. We quickly made a cucumber salad. It’s made with simple ingredients: sliced cucumber, sliced red onion, dressing from mayo, vinegar, sugar, and dill. Mix it all up together and serve. The kids were curious about them too, since they had helped with different parts of the garden throughout the spring. Looking back over the past few months, I realize how much I have learned through trial and error. At the beginning I was mostly following ideas from videos online without really understanding why certain things worked.Now I feel like I have a better sense of what the plants actually need and how small changes can affect their growth. There are still many plants in the garden that have not produced anything yet, so the season is far from over. But harvesting those first cucumbers felt like a good reminder that the effort has been worth it. I’m already starting to think about what I might do differently next year now that I have a little more experience.



Task:
 

Based on the gardening journal, what patterns show how the gardener's behavior and understanding changed over time?

Based on the journal entries, the gardener's behavior and understanding evolved significantly over time, showing a clear progression from novice enthusiasm to knowledgeable and resilient practice. Here are the key patterns that illustrate this change:

### 1. From Passive Following to Active Experimentation and Adaptation
*   **Initial State:** The gardener began by meticulously following instructions from TikTok videos ("superior way to start plants") with minimal prior knowledge. Initial attempts were imperfect (using packing tape that didn't stick).
*   **Evolution:** Over time, the gardener began to observe problems and actively seek solutions. Instead of just following videos, they adapted based on personal experience.
    *   **Example:** After noticing soil drying out, they switched from top-watering to a bottom-watering tray system.
    *   **Example:** Upon seeing faded leaves, they researched nutrient deficiencies and began creating "manure tea" from rabbit manure.
    *   **Example:** After the watermelon snail fell, they started a new one in a shorter, more stable format to prevent a repeat accident.

### 2. Increasing Problem-Solving Skills and Emotional Resilience
*   **Initial State:** The gardener expressed anxiety about whether the seeds would sprout and felt "crushed" by the loss of the first watermelon plants.
*   **Evolution:** The gardener developed a robust ability to identify, research, and solve problems, both horticultural and environmental. They also became more resilient in the face of setbacks.
    *   **Examples of Problem-Solving:** Managed a gnat problem by adjusting watering, identified and manually removed caterpillars (an organic pest control method), built a fence to deter deer and rabbits, and installed a greenhouse to manage temperature and humidity.
    *   **Examples of Resilience:** After losing most of the watermelon plants, they realistically assessed the situation and started over, realizing there was still time in the season. They viewed the accident as a valuable lesson.

### 3. Growth in Technical Knowledge and Practical Skill
*   **Initial State:** The gardener's knowledge was limited to the basics of creating a "seed snail."
*   **Evolution:** Through trial and error, research, and hands-on experience, their knowledge expanded immensely.
    *   **Horticultural Knowledge:** Learned about soil nutrition (hot vs. cold manure), the importance of hardening off plants, pollination, and the different growth habits of various plants (e.g., vining cucumbers vs. bushy peppers).
    *   **Practical Skills:** Gained skills in assembling a greenhouse, tilling soil, transplanting, building simple trellises, staking plants, and identifying pests.

### 4. Shift from Reactive Care to Proactive Planning
*   **Initial State:** The gardener reacted to issues as they appeared (e.g., covering snails with bags after they dried out).
*   **Evolution:** The gardener began to anticipate challenges and implement preventative measures.
    *   **Example:** Built a greenhouse not just for growth but to create a controlled environment.
    *   **Example:** Installed a fence after seeing animal tracks, proactively protecting the future garden.
    *   **Example:** Implemented the "hardening off" process to prevent transplant shock, a direct response to a previous lesson learned.

### 5. Expansion from Solo Project to Family Collaboration
*   **Initial State:** The project was a personal endeavor ("my journal").
*   **Evolution:** Gardening became a shared family activity. The gardener involved the children in choosing seeds, helping with assembly, digging, watering, and celebrating the harvest. This turned a chore into a bonding experience and a way to teach children about food and nature.

### 6. Deepening Connection and Understanding of Nature
*   **Initial State:** The goal was to be self-reliant and save money.
*   **Evolution:** The gardener developed a deeper appreciation for the complexities of nature. They noted the subtle differences in seedlings, observed the balance of a greenhouse ecosystem, and recognized the interconnectedness of plants, pollinators, and pests. The final entry reflects a profound sense of accomplishment and connection, culminating in the joy of harvesting and eating the first vegetables.

In summary, the journal depicts a journey from a beginner who followed online trends to a knowledgeable, observant, and resilient gardener who understands that success comes from adapting to challenges, learning from mistakes, and working in harmony with the environment.

source_rubrics: The response should clearly state that it is unlikely that the watermelon plants would have failed if the seedlings had not fallen from their tray.
The response should explicitly state that the biological principle the gardener was missing in February was acclimatization or "hardening off."

The response should compare the wind conditions of February 19th and when the gardener successfully transplanted the plants in April: some wind was mentioned in the April 14th entry, but no problems with wind were mentioned in the February 19th entry.
